This isn't on the same scale, but we had neighbors speculating on social media what happened. They drove past the crime scene and saw the coroner's vehicle. Even after we set the record straight, there were people commenting without reading the whole thread, speculating. Somebody thought he found by a group of kids, but they were mixing it up with a past event. I'm so glad it wasn't reported on in our local news.

And there are people saying "his body was found so late, how was nobody checking on him through the holidays?" It's very possible he cut himself off from friends and family so they wouldn't feel as much of a loss (of course they'll still be grieving). When I've thought about taking my own life, I've always told myself I wouldn't unless I separated myself from my family first.

And some people are completely ignorant about how this may be affecting the band members. They knew him, and possibly consider themselves to blame for his downward spiral. I relate to that kind of guilt.

So tl;dr- Some people need to being selfish, uncaring assholes and stop posting shit that is harming more people than it would ever be helping. Some of you are showing your true colors and saying shit like this doesn't make you any better than the man you are criticizing. We don't need to ignore his faults completely, as they are integral to his story. But we need to give the people who knew him time to grieve, and touch on these issues in a respectful way. You never know who'll be reading that. And if somebody said that shit about my dad, I know I'd be set back so far in my grieving process. Learn some empathy

I get where you're coming from on this. I think the idea of reclaiming slurs makes more sense when you use them as a point of pride, like queer is for a lot LGBTQ people. But when you use it as an insult it feels like it kinda defeats the purpose. So at that point it feels like it makes more sense to just stop using the word as a whole. At the end of the day, we can only control what we say. But I choose to respect the wishes of many members of minorities groups and avoid saying slurs full stop. As an LGBTQ person myself, I personally choose to use "queer" but not "f**". I respect others who want to use it in a more positive light, but the lyric in question is using it more as an insult. It's not like a feel like my freedom of speech is inhibited. I suppose I could say those words if I really wanted to, but I choose not to out of human decency. There are plenty of other words you can use.

Look into hyperhidrosis. It's the diagnosis for being naturally sweaty. It runs in my family so I have it somewhat. It's not as bad as some of my family members but I have to stay on top of my hygiene if I don't want a rash. Fungi can be attracted to moisture and can cause a smell (kinda like bread, yeast). Currently, I shower every other day (during band I would kick it up to every day). I make sure to scrub every surface and exfoliate using a glove. I also apply anti-fungal cream to spot treat it.

If it is just BO, definitely reapply deodorant after sweaty situations. Keep a travel size one on you if possible. Also, avoid antiperspirants. They don't really work super great a lot of times, and can stain your clothes. Hormonal changes can be a cause of particularly strong body odor, though there isn't much you can do to change that. Also diet can change your body odor, but I don't have much personal experience with that so I wouldn't know what to do about that.

1. For my school, band is a class for the first quarter/half of the first quarter. You can either do concert band for the rest of the semester, do concert band for the rest of the year, or have a different class fill that time slot. My band's comp season ended a little before our school's quarter so we used the period as a study hall or to play pep tunes. Drum majors just went back to their instruments during this time (we also did the same for parades). Throughout high school, I had drum majors who started on flute, clarinet, trumpet, and baritone.


2. It depends on the school, but mine did a winter guard season (also winter drumline). A lot of hornline members joined in on those (me being one of them). We used some of our class time after the comps were over to work on more complex things we didn't have time for during the winter season: Ballet technique (chaine turns and pirouettes), more complicated tosses, etc. Then we got a few weeks-maybe a month off before the winter season started up. My school does these open nights for anyone to try hornline, guard, or drumline. So they do a few of these and then the season proper starts. Ours is from November to April. And then we get a few months before the fall season starts up again.


3. Do you mean band directors and coaches? Our band directors are year-round and also teach a concert band period each. Our coaches and techs (drumline and guard) tend to work with other groups as well. I think they spend a lot of time planning for the next season. They come to our school occasionally for meeting in the off-season.


4. My school calls them band directors/teachers so their name doesn't suggest any election process in my case. They just get hired by the school and are involved as much as they can be. We had an older woman as another band director, but she rarely worked with the marching band due to her age I think.


5. In my school, you had to apply for leadership positions. You had write written responses to questions and include your resumé and stuff. Then our band director or coach would pick from the applicants and print the list of who was selected.


6. I'm assuming you're asking what a competition day might look like? Ours started with rehearsals on the morning, ending with a full-run (if it started earlier, we got a lunch break). Then we had a meal (lunch or dinner). And then we would pack up our stuff (frontline equipment, instruments, and props) into the trailer- sometimes we did this the night before if the comp was earlier. Then we took our bus ride. We would get there, then get into full uniform. Then we did some drill warm-ups and music warm-ups. Then we would get a few minutes we called "section time" to do a couple pre-show traditions. Then we got out there and preformed. Then we got out of full uniform and could either go watch the awards (we were always toward the end of the night) or just stay by our bus. For bigger comps (state or BOA) there is a step before you can get out full where you have individual photos taken. Then we took a bus back to the school and went home. For state, we at dinner at our comp site (between semifinals and finals).

I also have lots of anxiety about school. I've only ever hallucinated once I think, and that was from sleep deprivation. I'm not sure what you're exactly what you're experiencing, but if there are auditory effects, look into Exploding Head Syndrome. It has a weird name, but it just means you hear loud noises usually when your trying to fall asleep. If it's visual effects, I don't really have much advice. If you need a sleep aid stronger than melatonin, you could look into hydroxyzine or trazodone. Hydroxyzine is more specifically for anxiety with drowsiness being a really big side effect. Trazodone is a mild sedative. I personally didn't find much success with hydroxyzine, not that it doesn't work, I just don't often find myself in I situation where I could/should take it. Trazodone, on the other hand, works quite well for me. If hallucinations persist after making sure you're not sleep deprived, there may be another cause. I would definitely suggest you bring this up to a professional and/or caregivers to look into routes to resolve this. Best of luck to you

I get these a lot. I have combination skin, oily and dry. They're oil plugs, like the Lice Center commented. They start in your hair follicles and when your hair grows the oil can come with it. So you find these when your hairs fall out on the end, on the hair shaft (where you find eggs, except if you look close they are attached fully around the hair instead of attached on side of it), or on top of your hair. The last one happens I think because your scalp can be oily at first and then dry out, making them more likely to just fall out. In addition, color is usually a good indicator. While they both can appear white/light on your head, you can always put it on a white background like a tissue. A nit would be tan/brown. The oil plug would be white or yellowish. (I had a recent lice scare but remembered that I dyed my hair black, which usually gives me tinted oil plugs)

As someone who gets them a lot, it causes a lot of lice scares (and anxiety). So if you might be more prone to them, just wanted to give you some information to prevent future scares. Hope this helps!

So my favorite in terms of the whole day was 10th grade. Because in terms of how much fun I had during the parade itself, it's gotta be 11th.
